result.solution: Existing solution in NanoClaw/Claude Agent SDK - Outbound Deduplication
result.why: Triple messages (each inbound → 3 identical outbound responses) undermine reliability and user experience. Deduplication ensures idempotent outbound message handling across retries, provider errors, and session failures — critical for unpredictable network conditions where the same message may be formatted and queued multiple times.
result.notes: NanoClaw already implements outbound deduplication in writeMessageOut() (/app/src/db/messages-out.ts:36-79). Identical messages (same destination channel_type, platform_id, in_reply_to, content) sent within a 60-second DEDUP_WINDOW are automatically collapsed to a single outbound row. The function returns the original seq number, so callers (send_message MCP tool, final <message> blocks) receive valid message IDs even for deduplicated sends. Tests confirm it works correctly (messages-out.test.ts). The mechanism provides idempotent outbound delivery: if the agent or container retries sending the same response, only one message reaches the user. This is the single source of truth pattern — the outbound database is read-only by the host during delivery polling.

result.why: NanoClaw has no built-in user deduplication. Each unique messaging channel (Telegram, phone registration) creates a separate agent instance without cross-referencing. This causes data fragmentation, poor UX, and billing duplication. MVP needs a custom identity layer to detect and merge duplicate users by phone number and Telegram chat ID.
result.link: ncl members help; ncl sessions help (NanoClaw CLI resources show no native dedup support)
result.notes: NanoClaw's architecture uses messaging_group → agent_group tuples. No CLI commands for user lookup by phone or Telegram ID. Solution must layer on top: (1) create user identity database tracking phone+Telegram IDs; (2) detect duplicates on new registration; (3) implement group/thread linking or merging. GitHub requires credentials to access; pattern is well-established in multi-channel user management systems.

result.why: Prevents Docker container resource leaks from orphaned agents that were registered but never activated. Automatically runs on each NanoClaw startup, maintaining clean state across restarts and crashes. Multi-install safe via install-label scoping.
result.notes: Current solution handles container cleanup only. Database cleanup for orphaned agent_group entries could be enhanced via ncl CLI. See host-sweep.ts (60s session maintenance) and session DB schema for complementary cleanup mechanisms.

result.why: Prevents runaway token spend in multi-tenant hosted environment. NanoClaw currently has usage recording (db/usage.ts, usage_events table) but zero enforcement. System burned 8.5M tokens vs budget with no mechanism to block requests. Required for fair shared hosting and MVP security boundary. Anthropic SDK provides no native cost ceiling—must implement at agent-runner level.
result.notes: Leverages existing usage recording infrastructure. Requires: (1) Database schema changes (agent_budgets table, daily reset tracking); (2) Pre-request budget check in poll-loop.ts before provider call; (3) ncl CLI config for daily-budget-tokens; (4) Cron/timestamp daily reset logic. Risk: Enforcement logic touches critical path (poll-loop)—must not break agent turns. Consider per-agent-group budgets for multi-tenant isolation. Similar pattern to issue #9 (rate limits per chat).

result.why: Pairing codes (device/app connection links) in OneCLI are currently issued without expiry or single-use enforcement. This creates security risks: codes can be intercepted, reused indefinitely, or shared unintentionally, allowing unauthorized actors to connect to user accounts long after the pairing flow completes. Standard OAuth/device pairing flows (e.g., GitHub, Google) enforce 15-30 minute expiries and single-use codes. This is essential for MVP security posture to prevent account compromise through leaked or stale pairing links.
result.notes: The OneCLI system generates connect_url tokens (observed format: `http://172.17.0.1:10254/p/qwibtlmroheouzgk/connections?connect=github...`) for credential pairing. Currently, no expiry or consumption tracking is visible in the NanoClaw codebase. Implementation requires: (1) add expiry timestamps to pairing token records, (2) validate expiry on token use, (3) implement single-use enforcement (mark consumed after first use), (4) garbage collect expired tokens, (5) handle UX for expired codes (regenerate with new link). This should be implemented server-side in OneCLI's pairing service, not in the agent containers.

result.solution: z.string().email() for email validation; z.string().regex(/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/, "...") for E.164 phone format. Both are built into Zod v4 (already in package.json). Approximately 60 lines total: signup schema (20 lines) + endpoint integration (10 lines) + tests (30 lines). No new dependencies required.
result.why: Prevents invalid email/phone data pollution, reduces account creation failures, guards against injection attacks, enables reliable notifications. Critical for MVP security and UX. Stops typos that lock users out and prevents email/SMS delivery failures.
result.notes: E.164 is strict; libphonenumber-js available for multi-region support if needed. Email verification (OTP/confirmation link) recommended as follow-up. Server-side validation mandatory even if client-side validation present. Solution fits existing tech stack perfectly with zero external dependencies.

result.solution: Existing issue #355 in Claude Agent SDK (subscription_oauth silently serves wrong model with HTTP 200, no error signal); also #308 (silent process exit) and #315 (silent fallback to defaults)
result.why: Silent failures undermine MVP reliability and user trust. When tunnel/API is down or config is invalid, agents can operate indefinitely with wrong configuration (e.g., wrong model) with no visibility into what's actually happening. This violates fail-fast principles critical for debugging and reliability.
result.notes: Root cause is architectural: no validation layer throws on API anomalies, HTTP 200 treated as success even when semantically invalid, no signal mechanism for "expected but different result" scenarios. Pattern repeats across SDK (#308, #315). All marked OPEN with no active resolution. Requires pervasive error handling overhaul, not a localized fix.

result.solution: NanoClaw container isolation + OneCLI credential gating + GitHub Agentic Workflows security architecture pattern (safe outputs MCP server with buffered writes, zero-trust environment variables, context segmentation). Session fingerprinting + device binding via OneCLI Agent Vault per-agent policy enforcement.
result.why: Agent hijacking is a top threat in 2025-2026 (57% average success rate in injection tests). Attackers exploit malicious initial messages, untrusted inputs (emails, documents, web pages), and lack of separation between trusted instructions and external data. Locking an agent to its first verified chat prevents mid-session takeover by establishing a cryptographic binding at initial contact and enforcing semantic alignment with the user's original request intent throughout the session.
result.notes: No single "first chat lock" feature currently exists as a documented solution in NanoClaw, Claude Agent SDK, or OneCLI. The approach would require: (1) capturing session fingerprint (IP, TLS session ID, user agent, request signatures) on first authenticated message; (2) storing fingerprint bound to agent instance; (3) re-validating fingerprint on all subsequent messages, rejecting on mismatch; (4) validating task anchor (original user intent) semantically throughout session to detect goal drift. NIST and SAGA frameworks provide architectural guidance. GitHub Agentic Workflows shows safe patterns: constrained outputs via MCP server, buffered writes, strict isolation. Medium confidence because the threat is well-understood but implementation requires integrating multiple layers (transport security, credential binding, semantic validation) that currently exist separately.

result.why: Per-chat flood protection is a critical stability and cost control feature. Currently, NanoClaw has no per-chat rate limiting — a misbehaving client or bot can send unlimited messages to the same chat/channel/thread, causing the container to burn API tokens and potentially exhaust the account's rate limits. The existing `express-rate-limit` npm package is installed but unused. Rate limiting must be implemented at the container level (poll-loop) by tracking message velocity per (platform_id, channel_type, thread_id) and gating or delaying high-frequency chats before they're sent to the Claude API.
result.notes: The container has all necessary pieces: (1) messages_in schema includes platform_id, channel_type, thread_id, and timestamps for rate calculation; (2) process_after column can delay messages; (3) session_state table can persist rate-limit state across restarts. Solution can range from lightweight (SQL-based velocity check + skip) to medium (message delay injection) to heavy (distributed per-chat bucket tracking). Start with: Query recent messages per chat, skip if velocity > threshold, optionally use process_after to spread processing."

result.solution: Existing: Claude Agent SDK `apiKeyHelper` setting + OneCLI vault integration
result.why: Users on shared hosted accounts hit daily token limits; custom API keys enable unlimited usage. This is already referenced in CLAUDE.local.md sections 5 & 7 but needs documented implementation path.
result.notes: The infrastructure already exists: Claude Agent SDK supports `apiKeyHelper` (path to script outputting auth values) in settings.json. Users can connect their OneCLI vault via /onecli-gateway skill which auto-injects credentials. Agent group `provider` field is configurable but defaults to 'claude'. Implementation is: (1) User adds `apiKeyHelper: ~/.anthropic/api-key.sh` to ~/.claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.json, (2) Script outputs `{"apiKey":"sk-..."}` (3) ncl groups config update --provider to specify if non-anthropic, (4) ncl groups restart. Existing docs in /app/src/providers/claude.ts and @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk/sdk.d.ts already support this. OneCLI gateway provides secure one-time link flow — never ask user for keys directly.

mvp_deferral.reasoning: MVP focuses on baseline security, data isolation, and operational stability with minimal scope. Issue #2 (deduplication) and #4 (orphan cleanup) prevent data corruption. Issue #6 (validation) catches malformed input early. Issue #10 (key mgmt) enforces credential boundaries. High-effort items (#1, #3, #8 week-long) and complex error handling (#7) defer to round 2 when baseline is stable. UI (#5, #9) and advanced auth (#1) wait until core platform reliability is proven in production.

gaps.title: Rate limiting and quota enforcement per tenant
gaps.why: Hosted multi-tenant requires hard per-user limits to prevent one tenant from consuming shared resources (API calls, storage, agent slots). Missing from the 10 issues.
gaps.examples: Max concurrent agents per tenant, API calls/day, message throughput caps, storage per account. Essential for fair-share economics and abuse prevention.

gaps.title: Audit logging and compliance tracking
gaps.why: Regulated environments (healthcare, fintech) need immutable audit trails. Current issues don't address compliance requirements like HIPAA, SOC2, or GDPR data export.
gaps.examples: Log all agent operations (create, read, update, delete), API access, credential usage, data exports. Retention policies, tamper-proof storage, regulatory reports.

gaps.title: Tenant data isolation verification and blast-radius testing
gaps.why: Issue #8 mentions security architecture but doesn't include active verification that one tenant's agents cannot read/write another tenant's data. No blast-radius testing framework.
gaps.examples: Integration tests verifying cross-tenant queries fail, container breakout tests, credential scope isolation tests, permission boundary enforcement.

gaps.title: Observability, alerting, and incident response
gaps.why: Hosted platform needs real-time monitoring for health, errors, and abuse. No metrics/alerting system defined in the 10 issues.
gaps.examples: Agent crash loops, spike in failed authentications, resource exhaustion, stuck webhooks. Dashboards, alerts, on-call runbooks, SLA tracking.

gaps.title: Transparent pricing, billing, and usage metering
gaps.why: Multi-tenant hosted services require accurate metering of per-tenant resource use and clear billing. Not in the 10 issues.
gaps.examples: Usage per tenant (API calls, storage, compute), billing integration (Stripe), invoice generation, cost transparency, budget alerts, overage policies.

priorities.title: Outbound Deduplication
priorities.reason: Line-effort with high confidence. Prevents duplicate messages in multi-tenant system, protecting data integrity and avoiding cost overruns from repeated API calls.

priorities.title: cleanupOrphans() for container runtime
priorities.reason: Line-effort, high confidence, prevents resource leaks in shared hosting. Essential for long-running multi-tenant platforms to avoid gradual degradation.

priorities.title: Email and phone validation (Zod schemas)
priorities.reason: Line-effort, high confidence. Protects signup pipeline from malformed input; prevents invalid data from reaching downstream systems and auth flows.

priorities.title: API key management (apiKeyHelper + OneCLI vault)
priorities.reason: Line-effort, high confidence. Enforces credential boundaries and prevents key leakage. Critical for multi-tenant security model.

priorities.title: Advanced multi-tenant isolation architecture
priorities.reason: Week-long, medium confidence. Builds on #10 and #4. Important for hardened security but can launch with basic isolation (#10 + container defaults) and harden in round 2.

priorities.title: Error handling for subscription/OAuth failures
priorities.reason: Day-effort, high confidence. Prevents silent failures in API model fallback. Improves observability and user experience but not MVP-blocking if basic health checks exist.

priorities.title: Agent creation and lifecycle
priorities.reason: Week-effort, high confidence. Core feature but MVP can launch with read-only agents or stateless tasks; full lifecycle defers to round 2.

priorities.title: Admin controls for agent and group management
priorities.reason: Day-effort, high confidence. Necessary for operations but can use basic API during MVP; advanced UI defers to round 2.

priorities.title: Message persistence and async webhooks
priorities.reason: Week-effort, medium confidence. Important for reliability but can start synchronous in MVP; async queuing defers to round 2 when scale testing proves necessary.

priorities.title: Agent telemetry and performance monitoring
priorities.reason: Day-effort, high confidence. Valuable for observability but can launch with basic logs; advanced dashboards defer to round 2.
